citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., and Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. NAACL 2019.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova (Google AI Language, University of Washington)
description: BoolQ (Boolean Questions) is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question gathered from anonymized Google search queries, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article containing the answer, the article title, and a yes/no answer label. The dataset is split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
name: BoolQ
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated; the paper states "we elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets in order to be able to gather a larger dataset")
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Where there was disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement, creating "gold-standard" labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) They decided if the question is "good" — comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information — before seeing the Wikipedia page. (2) For good questions, annotators found a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question; questions could be marked "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information. (3) Annotators marked whether the question's answer is "yes" or "no". Each example was singly annotated (one annotation per item) to allow gathering a larger dataset, given that annotation quality assessment showed 90% accuracy against gold-standard labels.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset has a class imbalance: "Yes" answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The paper notes a correlation between question topic/type and the likelihood of a "yes" answer, though this correlation is too weak to outperform the majority baseline. The questions are sourced from Google search queries, which may reflect biases in what users search for. The paper explicitly chose naturally occurring questions (rather than crowd-sourced question generation) to avoid annotation artifacts common in NLI datasets where crowd workers write hypothesis statements.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine using the pipeline from Natural Questions (NQ). Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words (e.g., "did", "do", "does", "is", "are", "was", "were", "have", "has", "can", "could", "will", "would") and are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page were then given to a human annotator for further processing. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with an additional 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set, reaching a total of 16k questions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine (yes/no questions), paired with Wikipedia articles returned as top search results. An additional 3k yes/no questions came from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has a class imbalance with "Yes" answers being slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The question categorization analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset was updated after the analysis was carried out. The dataset uses singly-annotated examples, which may introduce some annotation noise (approximately 10% error rate vs. gold-standard labels).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Yes/no questions were heuristically identified from Google search queries by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five search results. Questions not marked as having a yes/no answer were excluded. Each question was paired with the selected passage (rather than the entire Wikipedia document) to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable. Questions from NQ were always placed in the train set.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions in search engines. By using naturally occurring questions, the dataset ties model evaluation to real user needs. The paper demonstrates that yes/no questions can be very challenging even when gathered from natural sources, which has implications for building more robust NLU systems.
rai:dataUseCases: Reading comprehension and natural language understanding, specifically yes/no question answering. The dataset is intended to test a model's ability to make complex inferences from text, including entailment-like reasoning. It is also intended as a benchmark for transfer learning research in NLP.

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling beyond noting that annotators can mark questions as "not answerable" (which are then excluded from the dataset).
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The paper does not specify the timeframe during which data was collected.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; missing/unanswerable questions are excluded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation (augmentation, resampling, balancing) is described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No ML models or automated tools are described as being used in the annotation pipeline itself; heuristic filtering was rule-based (indicator word list), not ML-based.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper states queries are anonymized and aggregated; no personal or sensitive information is described as being collected.
